summary: Silas applies kinetic maintenance to an irrigation pipe plagued by galvanic corrosion, but Hector's arrival turns the focus back to planetary resonance.
science_vegetable: Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mn High-Entropy Alloy lattice stabilization against galvanic corrosion induced by twin-sun eddy currents and copper flange couplings.

sensory_palette.sight: Pearlescent Mycena lucentipes bioluminescence pulsing in the damp arboretum twilight.
sensory_palette.sound: The rhythmic, mocking drip of water on oxidized iron, cut short by the clang of a wrench.
sensory_palette.smell: Rich, dark soil mixed with the sharp, metallic tang of rust and ozone.
sensory_palette.tactile_temperature: Cool, damp air clinging to the skin, punctuated by the cold heft of a forged wrench.
sensory_palette.taste_optional: A faint, lingering coppery taste from the ionized air.

interactive_features.description: Assess the structural integrity of the high-entropy alloy pipe suffering from galvanic corrosion.
Navigate carefully through the delicate, bioluminescent fungal beds.
Apply blunt force to temporarily reseat oxidized particulates and halt the leak.

narrative_prose:
For a man who could persuade impossible metals to sing, the ordinary, stubborn silence of rust was a particular insult. There it was, on a length of pipe he himself had hammered into being, a faint, cancerous blush of oxidization that had conspired with the water it carried to stage a tiny, tireless rebellion.

One drop, at a time.

Silas knelt on the dark, rich soil of the arboretum, the air around him cool and sweet. All about him, the family's cultivated fungi cast a soft, pearlescent glow, a functional twilight by which one could read, or work, or simply watch a problem grow. The Mycena lucentipes clustered at the base of the irrigation line, their green bioluminescence pulsing in a rhythm that seemed almost mocking to his tired eyes. To anyone else, this was a garden. To Silas, it was a humidity chamber designed specifically to destroy his work.

He ran a thumb over the pipe. It was a Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mn high-entropy alloy, designed for extreme tensile strength and thermal stability. It should have been impervious. But the planet's atmosphere was rich in corrosive ions, and the magnetic flux of the twin suns induced micro-currents in the metal, accelerating the galvanic reaction at a molecular level. The lattice structure was compromised by a simple, ill-advised copper fitting he'd used in a rush.

He could, of course, fix it properly. The thought was a brief, exhausting film that played in his mind: the long walk back to the Forge, the patient fire, the precious stock of refined ore, the clang and sweat of shaping a new, flawless piece. It would take the better part of a day, a day stolen from his true work, from the glorious, maddening puzzle of his sympathetic alloys. He was so close to stabilizing the resonant frequency of the new shield generator plating.

All for a single drop of water.

He let out a sigh, a small cloud in the glowing air. There were other solutions. Less elegant, less permanent. With the practiced movement of someone who had chosen practicality over perfection many times before, he picked up a heavy wrench. He did not fit it to the joint. He simply raised it, measured the distance, and gave the pipe a firm, resonant whack.

Clang.

The dripping paused.

Silas waited, holding his breath. A moment of silence. Then, with a renewed and almost cheerful impertinence, the drop began to form again. He hated it, with the quiet, simmering hatred one reserves for a problem that is both simple and, for the moment, entirely unbeatable. Suddenly, the stress spiked. The urge to simply rip the entire irrigation system out and catalog every single pipe section by molecular weight washed over him. A Pisces Polarity Inversion tugged at the corners of his mind—a fleeting thought that perhaps the water *wanted* to be free, that the pipe was a cage—but he crushed the poetic intuition down under a layer of rigid empiricism.

A second set of footsteps, heavy and rhythmic, approached through the damp soil. Silas didn't have to look up.

"If you hit it any harder, you'll have two leaks," Hector said, grinning as he stepped into the soft green light.

Hector was practically vibrating, the air around him smelling faintly of ozone and charred wire from whatever he'd been doing at the Stormbreaker tower. He carried a heavy coil of insulated cabling over one shoulder.

"I was applying a kinetic shock to reseat the oxidized particulates," Silas muttered, the words a perfect, self-aware parody of his own mind. "It's a temporary measure."

Hector chuckled, dropping the cable with a heavy thud. "The particulates don't care what you call them. They'll still eat your pipe. And speaking of eating things, the primary blue dwarf azimuth is shifting. We're going to see a magnetic polarity shear jump to 4.8 by mid-shift."

Silas finally lowered the wrench and sat back on his heels. The leak was a problem for later. For tomorrow. A planetary magnetic anomaly, however, was a problem for now.

"I'll need to check the resonant frequency on the Forge shielding," Silas said, rising to his feet and wiping his hands on his trousers. He picked up the heavy coil of cable, taking it from Hector in a smooth, practiced motion of shared labor.

"Exactly," Hector grinned, slapping Silas on the shoulder. "Let's go harness a titan."
